meta.descriptionEn: In just over a year, a 415 km railway was forced through some of the harshest jungle and mountains in Southeast Asia. Surveyors had called the route impossible back in 1885. In 1942 the Japanese army decided to build it anyway. This documentary follows the Burma Railway from its first survey to its last spike: why it was built, how the engineers cut through rock at Hellfire Pass, how the famous bridge over the river was raised, and the huge workforce of civilians and prisoners behind it. We separate the real story from the 1957 film, and ask what remains today and what the world still owes to the forgotten builders.

Hum film ki kahani aur asal tareekh mein farq bhi batayenge. Poori documentary Urdu aur English mein dekhein.

articleEn: On 17 October 1943, in the dense jungle of Southeast Asia, two groups of workers were advancing toward each other, one from the south and one from the north. They were laying a railway line, and the two ends were due to meet at kilometre 263, near Konkoita. Today it is known as the Burma Railway, but local people and historians remember it as the Death Railway.

When the two sections joined, a copper spike was driven in. The commanding General, Eiguma Ishida, did the honours, and a memorial plaque was placed there. A holiday was declared for 25 October, and that day was chosen for the line's ceremonial opening. Japanese staff were to travel by train from Nong Pladuk to Thanbyuzayat.

The line was finished ahead of schedule, since the original target had been December 1943. That early finish makes the story all the more striking. It also raises three questions. Why was this railway built at all? How was work in such difficult jungle done so fast? And what is the truth about the famous bridge you may have seen in the film? Let us go back from that last spike at kilometre 263 and see where it all began.

articleEn: The idea of this railway is very old. By 1885 the British government of Burma had surveyed a route that could link Burma with Thailand. It ran through Three Pagodas Pass and followed the valley of the Khwae Noi river in Thailand. In Thai, khwae means stream or tributary and noi means small, so Khwae Noi means the little river. The line would have to run beside the river, cross hills, and sometimes cross the river itself. The route was judged too difficult and the plan went no further, because it passed through hilly jungle divided by many rivers.

About 57 years later, in 1942, that same route became a necessity of war. The Burma Railway was 415 kilometres (258 miles) long, running from Ban Pong in Thailand to Thanbyuzayat in Burma, which is now called Myanmar. It would complete a rail link between Bangkok and Rangoon, joining the railways already in place at both ends. Of the 415 km, 111 km (69 miles) lay in Burma and 304 km (189 miles) in Thailand. The route crossed hill country such as the Tenasserim Hills, where Hellfire Pass is found. Three Pagodas Pass lay on the Thailand-Burma border, and the railway had to go through it.

On paper it looked simple: two cities, one line, and jungle in between. On the ground it was quite different. Even today, rebuilding the whole route is not considered easy. Since the 1990s various proposals have been made to rebuild the full railway, but by 2021 none had become reality. One reason is that the upper part of the Khwae valley now lies under the water of the Vajiralongkorn Dam, and the surrounding area is hilly, so reconnecting it would need a great deal of tunnelling. The route that looked hard in 1885 is still not easy today. So why did Japan decide to build a railway on such difficult ground? The answer lies in the map of the war.

articleEn: At the start of the war Thailand was neutral. On 8 December 1941 Japan attacked it, and Thailand soon surrendered. It had to accept an alliance and became a staging point for the attack on Singapore. In early 1942 Japanese forces attacked Burma, and British forces soon gave in. Japan now had a new problem: how to get supplies and manpower to its army in Burma.

At that time Japan relied on the sea. Ships carrying supplies and troops sailed around the Malay Peninsula, through the Strait of Malacca and across the Andaman Sea to Burma. The trip was about 3,200 km long, and it was exposed to attack by Allied submarines. After the defeat at Midway in June 1942 the danger grew. So Japan considered an alternative: a railway from Bangkok to Rangoon, which could avoid roughly 2,000 miles of dangerous sea travel.

According to the historical record, the railway's purpose was to move troops and weapons for the Burma campaign. It was basically a wartime logistics project, and Japan saw it as a feasible alternative. Work began in earnest in June 1942. Its official Japanese government name was Tai–Men Rensetsu Tetsudō, meaning Thailand-Burma-Link-Railway, so the name itself spoke of joining two countries.

Rails, sleepers and other materials had to come from somewhere, and the answer lay in territories Japan controlled. Much of the construction material, including tracks and sleepers, came from dismantled branches of Malaya's Federated Malay States Railway network. More came from various rail networks in the East Indies. In effect, railways in one region were taken up to meet the war needs of another. Before full construction, preliminary work was done on airfields and infrastructure. The target was December 1943, so time was short.

The Burma Railway was not the only project. Southeast Asian workers also built the Kra Isthmus Railway from Chumphon to Kra Buri, and a line in Sumatra. The railway later carried 500,000 tonnes of freight, but the human cost of building it was far heavier. Japan needed thousands of hands for the work. Who were these people, and where were they brought from? We look at that next.

articleEn: Start with the Japanese soldiers. About 12,000 were assigned to the project as engineers, guards and supervisors. Among them were 800 Koreans. They also oversaw the POWs and civilian labourers. Conditions for the Japanese were far better than for the workers, yet about 1,000 Japanese personnel, eight percent, died during construction.

Now the Allied prisoners of war. Their movements began in May 1942 from Changi Prison in Singapore and other camps. On 14 May 1942, 3,000 Australians left Changi and reached the area near Thanbyuzayat by sea. They first worked on airfields and infrastructure. On the Thai side, in June 1942, 3,000 British soldiers travelled by train from Changi to Ban Pong, the southern end of the railway. On 23 June 1942, 600 British soldiers arrived at Nong Pladuk to build a transit camp, from which men would be sent on to the railway work camps. Later, some British prisoners from Singapore and the Dutch East Indies were brought in, and Dutch and other Allied prisoners were put to work too.

The largest group, however, was civilians. One source says more than 180,000 Southeast Asian civilians were forcibly recruited, while another estimates at least 250,000. The sources differ, and because records are incomplete the exact number is hard to establish. They included Javanese, Malayan Tamils, Burmese, Malayan Chinese and other Southeast Asians. About 90,000 Burmese and 75,000 Malayans worked on the railway.

At first local people in Burma and Thailand were employed, but there were not enough of them, so Japan took another route. In early 1943 advertisements appeared in Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies promising good pay, short contracts and housing for families. The promises did not bring enough people. Then forced recruitment began, especially in Malaya, where ordinary civilians, even children, were rounded up and detained. Plantation families were told to send their children to the railway. Young, healthy men were often abducted. According to one source, more than 100,000 Malayan Tamils were brought into the project, and about 60,000 of them never returned.

The start date is interesting too. One source says construction began on both the Burma and Thailand sides on 16 September 1942, while another says POWs started work on the railway in October 1942. Perhaps the reason is that preliminary work came first. That was the workforce. Now, where did all these thousands of people live in the jungle? In the next part we go inside the camps.

articleEn: Imagine yourself in a jungle camp. Construction camps were set up along the whole railway at intervals of 5 to 10 miles, each housing at least 1,000 workers. They were moved up and down the line as needed. Camps were usually named after the kilometre mark where they stood, so one camp was called 131 Kilo. Housing was open bamboo barracks with thatched roofs, each about 60 metres long, with an earth floor in the middle. A barrack held 200 men, which left each person only two feet of width.

The hardest period is considered to be the months from mid-spring to mid-October 1943, known as Speedo. It is called the most difficult time of construction, and the railway was finished ahead of schedule. Proper tools were lacking too. In remote places like Hellfire Pass, men cut through rock without suitable construction tools. In these conditions disease became a major problem. Malaria, cholera, dysentery and tropical ulcers, along with malnutrition, were common causes of death.

Outcomes were not all the same, though. Death rates among Dutch prisoners and internees were lower than among UK and Australian prisoners. One suggested reason is that many had been born in the Dutch East Indies or lived there for years, so they knew the environment better. Medical care also varied greatly. Many European and US doctors had little experience of tropical diseases. A group of 190 US personnel with a Dutch medical officer, Lieutenant Henri Hekking, had only nine deaths, while another group of 450 US personnel had 100 deaths. articleEn: We now reach one of the most famous and most difficult places on the railway: Hellfire Pass. In Thai it is called Chong Khao Kard, meaning Torn Valley Pass, and the Japanese knew it as Konyu Cutting. It is a cutting in the Tenasserim Hills, a path made by cutting through rock. It was about 75 metres long and 25 metres deep, the largest rock cutting on the whole railway. The area was very remote, and suitable tools were not available.

Why not a tunnel? A tunnel was possible, but it could be worked only from its two ends, whereas a cutting could be worked everywhere at once. So the cutting was chosen, even though it meant far more labour for the prisoners. Australian, British, Dutch and other Allied prisoners worked here 18 hours a day, alongside Chinese, Thai, Malay and Tamil civilians. At night, in the light of burning torches, the sight of weakened men at work looked like Hell, which is how Hellfire Pass got its name.

The cutting was finished in six weeks. In those six weeks, 69 prisoners were beaten to death by guards, and many others died of cholera, dysentery, malnutrition and exhaustion. One important fact is often overlooked: the most deaths here were among civilian labourers, who had been lured by false promises of good jobs. Most were Malayans, meaning Malaya's Chinese, Malays and Tamils. According to the source, their conditions were largely similar to those of the POWs.

Beyond this was the area called Hintok, meaning Falling rock. The highlands began here, so the railway had to climb gradually. Hintok had four camps. The river camp had British, Australian and Tamil sections, and the mountain camp held Australian, British and Dutch prisoners. Weary Dunlop commanded the mountain camp, where a bamboo fence was built to keep out tigers. The first prisoners arrived on 26 January 1943.

After Hellfire Pass came the Three-Tiered Bridge, a trestle bridge built to gain height. Then there was another bridge, 400 metres long, called the Pack of Cards Bridge because it collapsed three times during construction. In the end it was abandoned and replaced with an embankment. On 19 June 1943 cholera broke out in the Hintok mountain camp and 57 Australian prisoners died. Bridge collapses killed 31 prisoners, another 29 died because of guards' behaviour, and 130 sick prisoners were sent to Tarsao. The bridges were completed in August 1943.

In 1983 former POW Tom Morris set out to preserve Hellfire Pass. Today there is a museum there, and visitors can walk through the cutting. But the railway's most famous structure is not a cutting but a bridge. Which bridge was it, and what happened there?

articleEn: The most famous part of the railway was Bridge 277, built over the river near Kanchanaburi. People know it as the River Kwai bridge. At that time, however, this river was considered part of the Mae Klong. In the Thai section the main route followed the Khwae Noi valley. The British mispronounced Khwae as kwai, which in Thai means buffalo, and so the name River Kwai took hold among the English. In 1960 the stretch of river the bridge crosses was formally renamed Khwae Yai, meaning big tributary.

Who built the bridge? On 26 October 1942, British prisoners of war arrived at Tamarkan. At first 1,000 prisoners were put to the work, led by Colonel Philip Toosey, the senior Allied officer at the bridge. In February 1943 another 1,000 Dutch prisoners of war were brought to Tamarkan. Chinese, Malay and Tamil civilians also worked on the bridge.

Two bridges were actually built. The first was a wooden railway bridge, ready in February 1943. In June 1943 a more modern ferro-concrete bridge went up beside it. Both crossed the river running from NNE to SSW. The steel and concrete bridge had 11 curved-truss spans, which the Japanese army had brought from Java in 1942. The rest of the railway's materials also came from far away, with most of the tracks and sleepers taken from dismantled rail networks in Malaya and the East Indies. More about Toosey comes later; first, what happened to the bridge in 1945.

In 1945 a planned US attack was cancelled because of bad weather. Then on 13 February 1945 RAF aircraft bombed both bridges. Forced labourers repaired the bridge, and by April the wooden bridge was running again. On 3 April 1945 a USAAF Liberator attack damaged it. Repairs continued, and by the end of May both bridges were operational again. This did not last. On 24 June 1945 the RAF destroyed the railroad bridges, and the line stayed closed for the rest of the war.

After the war, two curved spans of the steel bridge were replaced with angular truss spans received from Japan as part of postwar reparations. That is why the bridge you see today has both curved and angular spans, which is its hallmark. Trains still cross it to reach Kanchanaburi, and near the bridge stand a memorial plaque and an old steam locomotive.
But as famous as the bridge became, its story was also told wrongly. Why did that happen? The answer lies in a famous film.

articleEn: In 1957 David Lean made The Bridge on the River Kwai, based on Pierre Boulle's novel The Bridge over the River Kwai. William Holden, Alec Guinness and Jack Hawkins starred. But both the novel and the screenplay were fictional, and the railway was only a historical backdrop. The story features a British officer, Colonel Nicholson, who agrees to build a strong bridge, seeing it as a sign of British superiority.

The reality was very different. Lieutenant Colonel Philip Toosey, the senior officer at Tamarkan, was not like Nicholson and did not believe in collaborating with the Japanese. Toosey tried to slow the work. He encouraged sabotage, termites were collected, and the concrete was not mixed properly. Julie Summers writes in her book The Colonel of Tamarkan that Boulle modelled Nicholson on his memories of collaborating French officers.

The film's Colonel Saito also has a real counterpart. Risaburo Saito was actually the camp's second in command, and prisoners regarded him as relatively fair. Toosey later defended him at his war crimes trial, and the two became friends. Some Japanese viewers also objected to the film.

As for the bridge itself, the one in the novel was not on the river then called Kwai. Boulle never visited the bridge. He knew the railway ran beside the Kwae for many miles, so he assumed the bridge would be on that river, which proved wrong. The film's final scene was not real either. The bridge's destruction is entirely fictional, and even in the novel the bridge suffers only minor damage. Survivor Ernest Gordon wrote in his 1962 book that, unlike the officers in the film, the real officers did not build the bridge willingly.

The writing of the film has its own story. Carl Foreman and Michael Wilson were on the Hollywood blacklist, so they had to work secretly in England. Credit went to Pierre Boulle, who did not speak English, and the Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay was also given to him. In 1984 the Academy corrected this mistake. The film was shot in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, and the bridge used was built near Kitulgala. It was the highest-grossing film of 1957 and won 7 Oscars at the 30th Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

So what is the lesson of the film? It is a powerful story, but it is not history. The real conditions for prisoners and civilians on the railway were far harsher. And now the final question: when the railway was finished, what remained? How many lives were lost, and how is it remembered today?

articleEn: Finally, the most important question: what was the human cost of this railway? More than 90,000 civilians and about 12,000 Allied soldiers died. The Commonwealth War Graves Commission estimates 80,000 to 100,000 civilian deaths. Civilian records were not preserved, so the figures are disputed.

After the war, 111 Japanese military officials were tried for war crimes, and 32 of them were sentenced to death. In 1946 the removal of the Burma section of the railway began. In October 1946 the Thai section was sold to the Thai government for £1,250,000. On 1 July 1958 the line in Thailand was completed as far as Nam Tok. Today about 130 km of it remains, and trains run there.

Allied servicemen's graves were moved to official war cemeteries, and Kanchanaburi War Cemetery holds 6,982 Allied military personnel. For Southeast Asian civilians, a pagoda was built at Wat Thaworn Wararam, with plaques in Chinese and Tamil. The names of thousands are unknown. The Hellfire Pass museum also reminds visitors of these sacrifices. Yet Southeast Asian workers generally received no compensation or reparations.

In 2025, during a construction project in Kanchanaburi, the remains of 106 Tamil labourers were found, and a Buddhist ceremony was held for their cremation. These discoveries have shed new light on forgotten mass graves and the stories of the Romusha labourers. Grassroots efforts are now mapping the railway's lost sections.

So what is the lesson? Behind the story of one famous bridge lay the unnamed labour and sacrifice of thousands of workers. How do you think history should be remembered, given the difference between film and reality? Tell us in the comments, and like and subscribe to the video.

shorts.titleEn: The Copper Spike That Finished the Burma Railway
shorts.text: 17 October 1943 کو جنگل کے بیچ ایک copper spike ٹھونکی گئی۔ اس ایک spike نے پوری railway مکمل کر دی۔ مگر اس کی قیمت کیا تھی؟ جنوب مشرقی ایشیا کے گھنے جنگل میں دو گروہ ایک دوسرے کی طرف بڑھ رہے تھے، ایک جنوب سے اور ایک شمال سے۔ دونوں کو kilometre 263 پر ملنا تھا، Konkoita کے قریب۔ یہ railway Thailand کے Ban Pong کو Burma کے Thanbyuzayat سے جوڑتی تھی، اور اس کی لمبائی 415 km تھی۔ جب دونوں حصے ملے تو commanding General Eiguma Ishida نے copper spike ٹھونکی اور وہاں ایک memorial plaque لگایا گیا۔ 25 October کو چھٹی کا اعلان ہوا اور اسی دن کو ceremonial opening چنا گیا۔ منصوبہ دسمبر 1943 تک کا تھا، مگر کام پہلے ختم ہو گیا۔ تو لوگ اسے Death Railway کیوں کہتے ہیں؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 17 October 1943 ko jungle ke beech ek copper spike thonki gayi. Is ek spike ne poori railway mukammal kar di. Magar is ki qeemat kya thi? Janoob mashriqi Asia ke ghane jungle mein do giroh ek doosre ki taraf barh rahe thay, ek janoob se aur ek shumal se. Donon ko kilometre 263 par milna tha, Konkoita ke qareeb. Yeh railway Thailand ke Ban Pong ko Burma ke Thanbyuzayat se jorti thi, aur is ki lambai 415 km thi. Jab donon hisse milay to commanding General Eiguma Ishida ne copper spike thonki aur wahan ek memorial plaque lagaya gaya. 25 October ko chutti ka elaan hua aur isi din ko ceremonial opening chuna gaya. Mansooba December 1943 tak ka tha, magar kaam pehle khatam ho gaya. To log ise Death Railway kyun kehte hain? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
In October 1943 two work groups met at kilometre 263 and a copper spike marked the completion of the Burma Railway, with a ceremonial opening on 25 October.
Why is it still remembered by such a grim nickname?

shorts.titleEn: Why Was This Cutting Named Hellfire Pass?
shorts.text: ایک cutting کو Hellfire Pass کیوں کہا گیا؟ Thai زبان میں اسے Chong Khao Kard کہتے ہیں، یعنی Torn Valley Pass۔ Japanese اسے Konyu Cutting کہتے تھے۔ یہ Tenasserim Hills میں تھی، تقریباً 75 میٹر لمبی اور 25 میٹر گہری، اور پوری railway کی سب سے بڑی rock cutting۔ علاقہ بہت دور دراز تھا اور مناسب tools بھی نہیں تھے۔ سوال یہ ہے کہ tunnel کیوں نہیں بنایا گیا؟ Tunnel ممکن تھا، مگر اس پر صرف دونوں سروں سے کام ہو سکتا تھا۔ جبکہ cutting میں ہر جگہ ایک ساتھ کام ہو سکتا تھا۔ Allied prisoners سے روزانہ 18 گھنٹے کام لیا گیا۔ رات کو جلتی مشعلوں کی روشنی میں کمزور مزدوروں کو کام کرتے دیکھ کر اسے Hellfire Pass کا نام ملا۔ مگر ایک اور حقیقت اس سے بھی زیادہ بھاری ہے۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek cutting ko Hellfire Pass kyun kaha gaya? Thai zubaan mein ise Chong Khao Kard kehte hain, yaani Torn Valley Pass. Japanese ise Konyu Cutting kehte thay. Yeh Tenasserim Hills mein thi, taqriban 75 meter lambi aur 25 meter gehri, aur poori railway ki sab se badi rock cutting. Ilaqa bohat door daraz tha aur munasib tools bhi nahin thay. Sawal yeh hai ke tunnel kyun nahin banaya gaya? Tunnel mumkin tha, magar is par sirf donon siron se kaam ho sakta tha. Jabke cutting mein har jagah ek saath kaam ho sakta tha. Allied prisoners se rozana 18 ghante kaam liya gaya. Raat ko jalti mashaalon ki roshni mein kamzor mazdooron ko kaam karte dekh kar ise Hellfire Pass ka naam mila. Magar ek aur haqeeqat is se bhi zyada bhaari hai. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Hellfire Pass was the largest rock cutting on the Burma Railway, about 75 m long and 25 m deep.
Learn why it was cut as an open cutting instead of a tunnel, and why it got its name.

shorts.titleEn: Is The Bridge on the River Kwai Really a True Story?
shorts.text: کیا The Bridge on the River Kwai واقعی سچی کہانی ہے؟ 1957 میں David Lean نے یہ film بنائی، Pierre Boulle کے novel کی بنیاد پر۔ اس میں William Holden، Alec Guinness اور Jack Hawkins نے کام کیا۔ مگر novel اور screenplay دونوں fictional تھے، اور railway صرف تاریخی پس منظر تھی۔ Film میں Colonel Nicholson ایک مضبوط پل بنواتا ہے۔ حقیقت میں Tamarkan کے senior officer Lieutenant Colonel Philip Toosey تھے، اور وہ Japanese کے ساتھ collaboration کے قائل نہیں تھے۔ Toosey نے کام سست کرنے کی کوشش کی۔ ایک اور راز بھی ہے۔ جس دریا پر پل دکھایا گیا، اصل پل اس پر بنا ہی نہیں تھا۔ وہ Mae Klong دریا پر تھا، جسے 1960 میں Khwae Yai کا نام ملا۔ تو یہ غلطی کیسے ہوئی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya The Bridge on the River Kwai waqai sachi kahani hai? 1957 mein David Lean ne yeh film banayi, Pierre Boulle ke novel ki bunyad par. Is mein William Holden, Alec Guinness aur Jack Hawkins ne kaam kiya. Magar novel aur screenplay donon fictional thay, aur railway sirf tareekhi pas manzar thi. Film mein Colonel Nicholson ek mazboot pul banwata hai. Haqeeqat mein Tamarkan ke senior officer Lieutenant Colonel Philip Toosey thay, aur woh Japanese ke saath collaboration ke qaail nahin thay. Toosey ne kaam sust karne ki koshish ki. Ek aur raaz bhi hai. Jis darya par pul dikhaya gaya, asal pul us par bana hi nahin tha. Woh Mae Klong darya par tha, jise 1960 mein Khwae Yai ka naam mila. To yeh ghalti kaise hui? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
The 1957 film was fiction using the Burma Railway as a setting. The real senior officer, Philip Toosey, was very different from Nicholson.
See what the film got wrong about the bridge.
